Reflecting on the crash, Perin told PA Sport: "We had made a small mistake in the first part. **LA RIOJA, Argentina (CNN)** — Drama, heartbreak, and pure attrition defined the 12th stage of the Dakar Rally on Thursday, as race leader Carlos Sainz crashed catastrophically in the blinding dunes of Fiambalá, forcing his retirement from the race and handing the overall lead to his Volkswagen teammate, Giniel de Villiers.

What was supposed to be a decisive step toward victory for Sainz turned into a nightmare just 79 kilometers into the 253-kilometer special stage between Fiambalá and La Rioja. 

Sainz, a two-time World Rally Champion who had dominated this year's event with six stage wins, drove his Volkswagen Touareg over a hidden four-meter (13-foot) ravine in the treacherous, silt-like sands. The vehicle plunged nose-first and flipped onto its roof.

While Sainz escaped major physical injury, his veteran French co-driver, Michel Périn, suffered a fractured shoulder. Medical helicopters were dispatched immediately to the scene. Due to Périn’s injuries, the duo was forced to officially abandon the rally, sending shockwaves through the bivouac.

### A Seismic Shift at the Top

The tragedy for Sainz opened the door for South Africa’s Giniel de Villiers, who capitalized on the chaos to win the stage and vault into the overall lead of the car category. Accompanied by co-driver Dirk von Zitzewitz, De Villiers navigated the treacherous white sands to finish the stage in 4 hours, 6 minutes, and 43 seconds.

However, De Villiers was quick to point out that celebrating felt secondary after surviving what many drivers are calling the most punishing stage of the entire South American tour.

"It is an awful feeling to see a teammate go out like that, especially Carlos, who was driving an incredible race," De Villiers told reporters upon arriving in La Rioja. "But this stage was pure survival. The navigation was without a doubt the most difficult I have ever experienced in my career. You could not trust what you were seeing. The roadbook barely matched the terrain in places, and the sand was so soft you were constantly on the verge of getting trapped or plunging into a blind drop."

American driver Mark Miller, also piloting a Volkswagen, finished second on the stage to move into second place overall, giving VW a 1-2 grip on the rally, albeit under dramatically altered circumstances.

Miller echoed De Villiers' sentiments regarding the extreme navigation hazards that claimed Sainz.

"It was an absolute nightmare out there today—a complete maze of canyon beds and soft dunes," Miller said. "The sun was high, washing out all the contrast, making it impossible to read the depth of the terrain. One second you're flat out, and the next, the ground just disappears under you. It wasn't about speed today; it was about navigating through a minefield. We are just lucky to be here at the finish line."

### Despres Dominates on Two Wheels

In the motorcycle category, France’s Cyril Despres put on a masterclass in dune riding, conquering the brutal Fiambalá navigation to claim his second stage win of this year's event. 

The Red Bull KTM rider expertly picked his way through the soft sand hazards that stumped so many of his competitors, finishing ahead of rival Marc Coma. While Spain's Coma still maintains a comfortable buffer in the overall standings, Despres’ victory in Stage 12 consolidated his second-place position overall and served as a reminder of his elite navigation skills when the conditions are at their most extreme.

"Today you needed instinct more than a engine," Despres said after crossing the line. "It was hot, dangerous, and very easy to lose your way permanently."

### The Road Ahead

With Sainz out, De Villiers now holds a 2 minute and 23 second lead over Miller in the general classification. With only two stages remaining before the grand finish in Buenos Aires, the pressure on the remaining drivers is immense. 

As the Dakar Rally leaves the notorious sand traps of Fiambalá behind, the competitors head toward San Juan on Friday for Stage 13—where navigation will remain critical, and no lead can be taken for granted.

# DAKAR RALLY REPORT: STAGE 12
### Agony for Sainz as Devastating Crash Hands De Villiers the Lead in Fiambalá

**LA RIOJA, ARGENTINA** — The 2009 Dakar Rally took a catastrophic turn on Stage 12 as race leader Carlos Sainz plummeted into a deep ravine, destroying his hopes of a maiden Dakar victory. The nightmare crash forced the Spaniard out of the rally, paving the way for Volkswagen teammate **Giniel de Villiers** to win the stage and inherit a shock lead in the overall standings with just two days remaining.

### The Incident: Disaster at Kilometer 79

Heading into the 253-kilometer special stage from Fiambalá to La Rioja, Carlos Sainz and co-driver Michel Périn looked untouchable. Driving the Volkswagen Race Touareg 2, "El Matador" had won six stages and built a comfortable **27-minute and 31-second lead** over De Villiers. 

However, the treacherous, soft sand dunes and hidden dry riverbeds (riachuelos) of the Atacama/Fiambalá region had one final trap waiting. 

Just **79 kilometers** into the stage, Sainz’s car crested a blind ridge at high speed and plunged into a hidden **4-meter (13-foot) deep ravine** that had not been clearly flagged as a major hazard in the roadbook. The violent nose-first impact shattered the front end of the Volkswagen.

Although Sainz desperately wanted to repair the car and press on, Périn was in excruciating pain and unable to continue. Under Dakar rules, a driver cannot proceed without their navigator, forcing the race leader to officially retire from the rally.

---

### De Villiers Capitalizes on VW Teammate’s Misfortune

South Africa’s **Giniel de Villiers** and his German navigator **Dirk von Zitzewitz** were the first to come across the scene of Sainz's wreck. Realizing the danger, De Villiers checked on his teammates before pressing forward through the blinding "fesh-fesh" dust and punishing rocks.

American **Mark Miller**, also driving for Volkswagen, finished second on the stage (+16:17), while **Robby Gordon** finished third (+25:27) in his massive rear-wheel-drive Hummer H3.

The result drastically reshaped the leaderboard: De Villiers jumped into 1st place overall, holding a **2:35 lead over Mark Miller**, giving Volkswagen a surprising 1-2 overall standing, albeit under bitter circumstances.

### Bikes Category: Despres Takes Stage, Coma Protects Lead

In the motorcycle category, Frenchman **Cyril Despres** (KTM) claimed the stage win, navigating the tricky Argentine dunes in 3 hours, 57 minutes, and 37 seconds. 

Overall leader **Marc Coma** (KTM) took a conservative approach to avoid the fate that befell Sainz. Coma finished second on the stage, dropping only a few minutes to Despres, and maintained a massive overall lead of over **1 hour and 29 minutes**.

#### **Carlos Sainz (Overall Leader, Retired):**
> *"We were driving normally, not over-pushing because we had a good cushion. Then, suddenly, the ground just disappeared beneath us. It was a four-meter drop into a riverbed that wasn’t properly marked as danger three in the roadbook. Michel hurt his shoulder very badly in the impact. > *"The impact was extremely violent. I immediately felt a sharp pain and realized my shoulder was dislocated. I tried to see if I could hang on, but every bump was excruciating.
